title: A conversation with Yale Law School Professor John Morley '06
description_text: Join us for a conversation with Yale Law School Professor John Morley '06 as he discusses his remarkable career and the business of Big Law. John Morley is Augustus E. Lines Professor of Law at Yale Law School and a theorist of organization. He studies how the law encourages — and discourages — cooperation. His research has probed the foundations of a wide variety of businesses and social groups, including ordinary corporations, investment funds, trusts, law firms, customer cooperatives, mutual financial institutions, marriages, cities, states, and nations. Morley is active in shaping real-world organizations. He was the primary drafter of the Anthropic Long-Term Benefit Trust agreement and has served since the Trust’s founding in 2023 as its principal legal counsel. He regularly advises major companies and institutions on challenging problems in governance, including public benefit mission commitments, mutual ownership governance, and AI safety. He has testified as an expert witness in proceedings related to trusts, investment funds, and general corporate organization. Morley has a special interest in the regulation and structure of investment funds. He has authored many articles on hedge funds, mutual funds, and private equity funds. He also has a focus on the law of trusts and estates. He served as the reporter for the Uniform Directed Trust Act, which has now been adopted by the legislatures of 22 states. Morley also writes and speaks frequently about the governance of law firms. With Joel Cohen, he co-hosts New Law Order, a popular podcast on the legal profession. He received undergraduate degrees in political science and economics from the University of Utah and his law degree from Yale Law School.

title: Small Structures, Big Impact: When Our Immune System goes Local
description_text: Speaker: Clémence Riffard, Immunobiology, YSM Our immune system is remarkably good at detecting threats and organizing a response to protect our body. The spleen and lymph nodes (our secondary lymphoid organs) act as gathering points where immune cells can recognize threats and coordinate their defense. But what happens when an organ or tissue is threatened locally? Can the immune system build its own defense hubs exactly where they are needed? This is the role of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS). These organized clusters of immune cells form in tissues during inflammation, and provide local environments where the immune defense can be orchestrated. In this course, we will take a closer look at these intermediate structures: from the discoveries that brought them to light, to the mechanisms that drive their formation and function in the body. Ultimately, we will ask what these structures mean for many patients and whether understanding them could help us better prevent or treat various diseases.

title: Scaling Biochar Solutions: From Field Observations to Global Modeling - CIE Lunchtime Series
description_text: Can biochar deliver consistent climate and agricultural benefits from individual fields to the global scale? Biochar, a carbon-rich material derived from biomass, has the potential to improve soil health, enhance agricultural productivity, and mitigate climate change. However, its effectiveness varies considerably across environmental conditions and management practices, raising questions about its long-term and large-scale impacts. In this seminar, Professor Wei Ren will present her team's research that integrates field observations, global data synthesis, and process-based ecosystem modeling to examine how biochar affects soil carbon storage, nutrient cycling, greenhouse gas emissions, and crop productivity. Together, these approaches help explain the environmental controls and underlying mechanisms shaping biochar responses across locations and over time, while identifying uncertainties in its long-term effectiveness. The seminar will also provide a basis for discussing how these findings can inform broader assessments of biochar deployment and carbon removal, with potential connections to industrial ecology and the bioeconomy. Dr. Wei Ren is an Associate Professor in the Department of Natural Resources and the Environment at the University of Connecticut. Her research focuses on understanding the interactions among climate change, human activities, and terrestrial ecosystems, with particular emphasis on carbon and nutrient cycling, ecosystem sustainability, and climate-smart agriculture. Her interdisciplinary research integrates field observations, remote sensing, global data synthesis, machine learning, and process-based ecosystem modeling to investigate ecosystem responses to environmental change and evaluate the effectiveness of sustainable land management practices across spatial and temporal scales. Her work aims to advance predictive understanding of ecosystem dynamics and inform science-based strategies for climate change mitigation and adaptation, sustainable agriculture, and natural resource management.

description_text: Environmental Agency in the Sahel: Making Sense of Change across Scales, Cultures, and Disciplines, a discussion with Professor Alessandra Giannini (Environmental Studies, NYU) Tuesday, November 10, 2026, 12:45-2:00, HQ 276 (320 York Street) In the early 2000s, Alessandra Giannini used climate models to demonstrate conclusively that the origin of the Sahelian droughts of the 1970s and ‘80s lay in subtle changes in the surface temperatures of the global ocean—not, as previously thought, in locals’ mismanagement of land through overgrazing, farming marginal land, or cutting wood for fuel. That demonstration not only “freed farmers of blame in Sahel drought,” as one news outlet put it. It also raised questions for interdisciplinary inquiry: Could local knowledge enable the regreening of the Sahel by making more efficient use of rainfall, providing a new model for adapting to climate change? Since then, further climate modeling has elucidated the role of pollution from fossil fuel combustion in effecting the oceanic change responsible for drought in the Sahel, implicating planetary-scale agency.

title: Beyond Prediction: Toward Trustworthy and Human-Centered GeoAI
description_text: Dear colleagues, Please join us for a presentation by Zhe Zhang, Associate Professor of Geography at Texas A&M University: Beyond Prediction: Toward Trustworthy and Human-Centered GeoAI Monday, November 30 12:00–1:00 p.m. Digital Humanities Lab • Building: Sterling Memorial Library (First Floor) • Street Address: 120 High St, New Haven, CT 06511 Lunch will be provided. Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) has expanded our capacity to model complex spatial and spatiotemporal processes, but critical challenges remain around uncertainty, explainability, heterogeneous data integration, and meaningful human decision-making. In this talk, Professor Zhang will explore advances in trustworthy, human-centered GeoAI across three connected areas: (1) uncertainty-aware GeoAI for transportation and infrastructure systems; (2) multimodal GeoAI for disaster and infrastructure resilience; and (3) spatiotemporal modeling and explainable AI that helps decision-makers understand the geographic, temporal, and contextual factors behind model outcomes. Professor Zhang’s work brings computational intelligence together with geographic context, domain expertise, and human knowledge to advance more transparent, collaborative, and context-aware spatial decision-support systems. About the speaker: Zhe Zhang is an Associate Professor in the Department of Geography at Texas A&M University, with joint appointments in Electrical and Computer Engineering and the Texas A&M Hazard Reduction and Recovery Center. Her research focuses on participatory GIS, spatial decision support, human–AI interaction, and trustworthy GeoAI. Her work has been supported by the NSF, NASA, USDOT, NOAA, and the National Geographic Society. She is the recipient of the NSF CAREER Award, the Distinguished Contributions Award from Women in GIS, and the 2022–2024 ISPRS Jack Dangermond Best Paper Award. We hope you can join us.

Entrusted to the Yale Peabody Museum, along with a century of correspondence and family albums, those archives proved indispensable to biographer Miriam Horn, whose Homesick for a World Unknown, The Life of George B. Schaller, was published in April by Penguin Press. title: BIOMES: "Sustainable AI – is it possible?" presented by Elaine Grunewald, Lecturer, Yale School of the Environment
description_text: About the Seminar: The AI value chain is extensive, complex and varied, ranging from minerals and materials, to hardware to infrastructure to models and user applications. There are distinct sustainability issues across this chain. Often the public associates AI sustainability issues to be data center centric, when in fact the picture is far more complex, encompassing energy and water issues, but also the profound effects on people, the economy and society more broadly. At the same time, the magnitude of the sustainability challenges we face, and the fact that we have exceeded several planetary boundaries - ranging from climate change to oceans to biodiversity – will likely require AI to solve. This talk will breakdown the issues, and outline the two sides of the sustainability AI coin – risk and opportunity – from a business lens, building on Elaine’s more than 2 decades of experience in the corporate sustainability space. About the Speaker: Elaine is a global operating executive with more than 25 years of experience leading technology-driven organizations through growth, transformation, and complexity across multinational, start up, and board environments. Her focus is on tech and digitalization, venture building and investing, public affairs and partnerships, and corporate development. Her advocacy for the private sector’s role in solving sustainability challenges has been a red thread throughout her career. She has held senior executive roles at scale, including Senior Vice President and Executive Team member at Ericsson, where she led global sustainability, public affairs, and stakeholder strategy and built an organization of 150+ professionals operating across regulated and geopolitically complex markets. In that role, she worked closely with the Board, CEO, investors, governments, and customers, positioning sustainability, trust, and responsible technology as drivers of long-term competitiveness and growth. More recently, she served as President of the Tonomus Venture Studio, the venture-building arm of NEOM, Saudi Arabia’s future-focused development. She led a global, multidisciplinary team responsible for building and launching a portfolio of AI- and data-driven ventures. Using a hands-on operating model, her team incubated and scaled early-stage companies across sectors including fintech and digital identity, workforce authentication, biotech, satellite-enabled services, climate tech, and responsible AI. Elaine co-founded two companies - the AI Sustainability Center, developing practical tools to help companies address the scaling of Responsible AI, and Emphco AB, a platform she uses to advise numerous companies, funds and CEOs and to make clean tech investments. Alongside operating roles, she brings board and capital-markets experience, having served on public company boards and as an independent director of a Nasdaq-listed SPAC. Non-profit boards include the Whitaker Peace & Development Initiative & the International Women’s Forum Sweden. She is the co-author of the book Sustainability Leadership, a Swedish Approach to Transforming Your Company, Your Industry and the World (2020, Palgrave Macmillan). She was also a contributor to the anthology Ethics at Work: Dilemmas of the Near Future and How Your Organization Can Solve Them (2022). Elaine is a frequent speaker including the World Economic Forum, United Nations, LEAP, SXSW, tech industry events and has been engaged in the Broadband Commission for Sustainable Development, and the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network. She has held guest lectures at multiple universities including Columbia University Business School and Sweden’s Royal Institute of Technology (KTH) Business School. She has received several awards for her work with sustainability and women's leadership.

title: Interwoven: Sounds and Visions from the World’s Refugee Camps
description_text: This retrospective exhibition of community art and traditional music will be on view at the Yale Institute of Sacred Music’s Miller Hall at 406 Prospect Street, New Haven from October 15 -December 3 on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays from 12 - 4 p.m., except for Thanksgiving week when the ISM is closed. Presented by Artolution, an international community-based public arts, education, and mental health organization that uses creative expression to build connection, resilience, and community, the exhibition is organized by Dr. Max Frieder, Artolution Co-Founder and Chief Creative Officer (read more about Dr. Frieder below). Building on the acclaimed exhibition Interwoven: Exchange Artworks Made Between Refugee Camps Around the World, originally launched at the United Nations, this expanded presentation hosted at the ISM brings together large-scale collaborative artworks, video documentation of traditional folkloric musicians, and cultural artifacts created by displaced communities across five continents. The exhibition creates a dialogue between visual art and music in contexts of displacement and crisis. Alongside the artworks, visitors encounter videos of musicians from the same communities, offering an opportunity to experience not only the remarkable stories behind the works, but also the sounds, movements, languages, rhythms, and creative traditions of the people who made them. Together, these works offer a powerful portrait of communities using art, music, and cultural expression to preserve identity, share their stories, and create connections across borders.

title: Dissertation Writing as Practice Series (Session 5): 12/1
description_text: This series provides dissertation writers with the structure, resources, and creative outlets to design and maintain a sustainable approach to writing. We will explore effective practices for pacing your dissertation writing while helping you overcome common writing blocks and find balance in your writing life. During each weekly live workshop session, we will engage with a relevant theme, discuss your writing practice and progress, and complete low-stakes reflective and creative activities to build your writing momentum. Invigorated by poetry, art, and other creative inspirations, and supported through discussion boards and supplementary resources, we will help you craft a writing practice to help you maintain, and even enjoy, a PhD writing life. As part of the resources offered in this series, students will receive access to tutorials on how to try Scrivener, a software program for organizing writing and brainstorming. Students who attend at least four of the six sessions will receive a free, lifetime Scrivener license. The weekly session themes are: 1. Time Management and Dissertation Planning (10/27) 2. Crafting a Holistic Dissertation Writing Practice (11/3) 3. Working through Distractions and Procrastination (11/10) 4. Writing through Imposter Stress (11/17) 5. Hanging up on Perfectionism and Demoralization (12/1) 6. Assessing Process & Progress + Long-View Spring Semester Planning (12/8) Intended Audience: ABD PhD students from all disciplines who have begun writing their dissertation.

title: Sealed Off
host_group: Yale Vermilion Theater for Students and Scholars
description_text: Join us for an unforgettable evening of theater at the Yale Vermilion Theater FA26 Showcase! Set in 1940s Shanghai, Sealed Off begins when a sudden military blockade brings a tram to a halt amid the turmoil of a city at war. Two strangers, Wu Cuiyuan, a university English teaching assistant, and Lü Zongzhen, a bank clerk, find themselves together in the crowded tram. She longs for genuine human contact; he seeks an escape from the monotony of everyday life. As their conversation unfolds, two individuals constrained by family, society, and the roles they are expected to play discover the possibility of connection in this fleeting moment of stillness. But when the blockade is lifted and the tram begins moving again, what will become of them? Adapted from Eileen Chang's short story of the same name, Sealed Off explores the delicate interplay between truth and illusion in human nature through a chance encounter between two strangers. It also raises questions about the complexities of love: Do we truly fall in love with another person, or do we simply long to be seen through their eyes? Amid the many constraints of reality, can we ever truly reach our authentic selves and one another? This production is supported by the Grace Hopper College Creative and Performing Arts Award. Production in Chinese (Mandarin) with English subtitles. The event is open to the public, with donations welcome (via Venmo @ChinYuan-Ong). We can’t wait to see you there!

title: Artist Talk | Richard Long on "Gravity"
description_text: In this special conversation at the Yale Center for British Art, acclaimed British artist Richard Long talks about his installation, "Gravity," a site-specific work conceived for the YCBA’s Entrance Court, with James Meyer, curator of modern art at the National Gallery of Art. This program is free to attend; registration is not required. --- About the speaker: Richard Long has been in the vanguard of conceptual art in Britain since he created A Line Made by Walking over half a century ago in 1967, while still a student. This photograph of the path left by his feet in the grass, a fixed line of movement, established a precedent that art could be a journey. Through this medium of walking, time, space, and distance became new subjects for his art. From that time he expanded his walks to wilderness regions all over the world, including a walk in the Alps that was documented by his first text work for the seminal exhibition of minimal and conceptual works titled When Attitude Becomes Form at the Kunsthalle Bern in 1969. After 1969, he began making journeys and sculptures in wilderness places all around the world. In the 1980s, Long began making new types of mud works using handprints applied directly to the wall. He also continued to make large sculptures of lines and circles from slate, driftwood, footprints, or stone, often sourced from quarries near the exhibition sites. Long mediates on his experience of these places, from mountains through to deserts, shorelines, grasslands, rivers, and snowscapes, according to archetypal geometric marks and shapes, made by his footsteps alone or gathered from the materials of the place. These walks and temporary works of passage are recorded with photographs, maps and text works, where measurements of time and distance, place names, and phenomena are vocabulary for both original ideas and powerful, condensed narratives. Long was born in Bristol, UK, in 1945 and he lives and works between London and Bristol. He studied at the West of England College of Art, Bristol (1962–65), then St Martin’s School of Art, London (1966–68).
